flawed_step: Step 4: From F∩Y=A, G∩Y=B, and A∩B=∅, it does not follow that F∩G=∅; F and G may intersect outside Y.
counterexample: The deleted Tychonoff plank Y=([0,ω₁]×[0,ω])\{(ω₁,ω)} is a nonnormal subspace of the normal space [0,ω₁]×[0,ω], with both ordinal intervals carrying their order topologies.
assessment_summary:
1. [Justified] Let X be normal, let Y⊆X have the subspace topology, and let A,B be disjoint closed subsets of Y. This is the appropriate setup for trying to prove hereditary normality.
2. [Justified] There are closed F,G⊆X such that A=F∩Y and B=G∩Y. This is exactly the characterization of relatively closed subsets.
3. [Justified] The hypotheses imply (F∩G)∩Y=A∩B=∅. Thus any intersection of F and G lies outside Y.
4. [Not justified] One cannot infer F∩G=∅: Step 3 excludes intersection only inside Y, so normality of X cannot yet be applied to F and G. This is the first failing step.
5. [Not justified] The proposed application of normality of X to obtain disjoint open neighborhoods of F and G depends on the unsupported claim in Step 4.
6. [Justified, conditional] If disjoint open sets U,V⊆X containing F,G had been obtained, then U∩Y and V∩Y would be disjoint relatively open neighborhoods of A,B. This follows directly from the subspace topology.
7. [Not justified] The attempted argument does not prove Y normal because the required ambient disjointness in Step 4 is unavailable.
8. [Justified] To determine whether this is merely a proof gap, let X=[0,ω₁]×[0,ω], where both ordinal intervals carry their order topologies, and put p=(ω₁,ω) and Y=X\{p}.
9. [Justified] Each ordinal interval [0,γ] is compact Hausdorff: Hausdorffness follows from the order topology, and compactness follows by transfinite induction, since a cover member containing γ contains a final segment and the remaining initial segment is compact by induction. Hence their finite product X is compact Hausdorff.
10. [Justified] Every compact Hausdorff space is normal and T1. Indeed, Hausdorffness makes singletons closed; for disjoint closed C,D, pointwise disjoint Hausdorff neighborhoods and compactness of D give, for each c∈C, an open neighborhood separated from an open neighborhood of D, and compactness of C reduces these to finitely many, producing disjoint open neighborhoods of C and D. Thus X is normal under the supplied definition.
11. [Justified] Define A={ω₁}×[0,ω) and B=[0,ω₁)×{ω}. They are disjoint subsets of Y.
12. [Justified] Both are closed in Y: A=Y∩({ω₁}×[0,ω]) and B=Y∩([0,ω₁]×{ω}), and the displayed ambient sets are closed in X.
13. [Justified] Let U be any relatively open neighborhood of A in Y. For each n<ω, openness at (ω₁,n), together with the fact that n is isolated in [0,ω], gives a countable ordinal α_n<ω₁ such that (α_n,ω₁]×{n}⊆U.
14. [Justified] Let α=sup_{n<ω}α_n. A countable supremum of countable ordinals is countable, so α<ω₁; consequently β=α+1 also lies below ω₁.
15. [Justified] If V is any relatively open neighborhood of B, then V contains (β,ω). Openness supplies a product neighborhood of this point containing (β,n) for every sufficiently large finite n.
16. [Justified] For every such sufficiently large n, β>α≥α_n, so (β,n) also belongs to U by Step 13. Hence U∩V≠∅.
17. [Justified] Thus the disjoint closed subsets A and B of Y have no disjoint open neighborhoods, so Y is not normal.
18. [Justified] Since the normal space X has the nonnormal subspace Y, the claimed hereditary property is false.
